title: Cable and rib scarf
subtitle: Alternating cable and rib panels across the full width.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat with three four-stitch cables alternating with four-stitch rib panels on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 22 cm wide by 175 cm long. The cable and rib panels alternate across the full width so neither side of the scarf is smooth: both faces show texture.
sourceNotes: Cable-and-rib combinations for scarves and comforters appear throughout Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive. The pattern of alternating cable and rib panels across the full width is documented as a standard scarf construction in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), citations only.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn. It finishes at 22 cm wide and 175 cm long. Alternating four-stitch C4F cable panels and 2x2 rib panels repeat across the full width. Three cable panels alternate with three rib panels, so neither face is plain when the scarf is folded.

Flat construction was chosen because the alternating cable and rib pulls both long edges inward evenly, producing a stable fabric that does not need a border to lie flat. The finished scarf needs about 420 m (approximately 240 g) of aran-weight yarn. The combined cable-and-rib compression produces a 22 cm wide scarf from 40 cast-on stitches that would give about 25 cm in plain stocking stitch. The scarf wraps once around the neck with both ends hanging at a comfortable chest length.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Smooth wool gives the clearest cable definition.

items.name: 5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 6 / US 8)

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. In the cable and rib pattern the gauge compresses to approximately 16 sts per 10 cm. Swatch the full cable-plus-rib arrangement, measure unstretched. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by about 1.4 cm. Row gauge drift across the full 385 rows changes the finished length by up to 15 cm.
Stitches used
K (knit), P (purl), C4F: slip 2 to cable needle at front, K2, K2 from cable needle. 2x2 rib: [K2, P2] across rib panels.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 40 stitches on the needle. The stitch layout is: [C4F panel (4 sts), 2x2 rib panel (4 sts)] x 5 = 40 sts across 5 pairs of panels. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 40 stitches: (15.7 x 40) / 10 + 15 = 62.8 + 15 = about 78 cm. Leave a tail of at least 78 cm.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 40 stitches on the needle.
Body
Row 1 (RS, cable row): [C4F, K2, P2] 5 times. (40 sts)
Row 2 (WS): [K2, P2, P4] 5 times -- i.e. work the rib stitches as P2, K2 (reading from WS) and the cable stitches as P4. (40 sts)
Row 3 (RS, plain): [K4, K2, P2] 5 times. (40 sts)
Row 4 (WS): as row 2. (40 sts)
Row 5 (RS, plain): as row 3. (40 sts)
Row 6 (WS): as row 2. (40 sts)
Repeat rows 1 to 6 until the scarf measures 175 cm from the cast-on edge. At the halfway mark (approximately row 193, around 87 cm), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 193 you should have 40 stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a stretchy bind-off in pattern on a right-side row to match the elasticity of the rib panels.
Common faults

Rib and cable panels swapping alignment after several repeats. If you begin a right-side row one stitch out, the cables land on the rib stitches. Use a stitch marker after the first 4-stitch cable panel to anchor the alignment from the start.

Cable panels all crossing in the same direction but one looking different from the others. Check that C4F is always worked with the cable needle held at the front. If one panel has the cable needle at the back, it will produce a right-leaning cross that is visually distinct from the others.
Bound-off edge narrower than cast-on. This is a too-tight bind-off on rib. Use the stretchy bind-off or bind off on a needle one size larger.
Finishing
Weave in both tails along the back of a rib column and trim close.
Steam blocking
settles the cable and rib panels. Hold the iron above the surface and allow steam to penetrate without pressing down. Leave flat.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry. Do not wring.
What to try next

From here the cabled cowl applies the same panels in the round, where the fabric is entirely knit on every round with no WS row complexity. The simple cable scarf removes the rib and uses a single cable on a plain ground for comparison.
